\footnotesize \textbf{Note:} Recognition and nonword conditions report accuracy at the 0.9 criterion, where an error is a nonword whose winning lexical unit reached threshold. The priming blocks report the proportion of primes that activated \emph{their own target's} unit above 0.5, following Dandurand et al.\ (2013, \S3.2); these are effects to be measured, not errors, and the prediction is SILE $>$ SLNE and SILNECE $>$ SILOPCE. Reduced item counts exclude degenerate transpositions, where the two swapped positions held the same letter so the stimulus is identical to the word it came from: 92 French, 563 Finnish and 74 FIN random items for letter transposition, and 105, 186 and 101 for transposed-letter priming. SILOPCE items are always valid but carry the same exclusion so the contrast is computed within-item.

 & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{\textbf{Proximity effect}} & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{\textbf{Letter cluster effect}} \\

\hline

\vspace{2mm}
\begin{minipage}{0.95\textwidth}
\footnotesize \textbf{Note:} Proximity is measured over the 156 off-diagonal cells of the 13 $\times$ 13 position matrix; letter cluster over the full letter-by-letter matrix (37 $\times$ 37 French, 23 $\times$ 23 Finnish). French versus Finnish: $F$(1, 310) = 198.48 and $F$(1, 1896) = 159.42, both $p < .001$. All three lower decks were trained for 421 epochs for this comparison. Criterion stopping otherwise halts each model at a different epoch, and longer training increases representational separation on its own; the random model scores 3.91 and 4.16 at its own 2000-epoch stopping point, above Finnish, but 2.92 and 3.24 when matched, below it.
\end{minipage}
\end{table}
